title: Allocation, mutation and alias-safe numerical work
outcome: Implement a preallocated matrix step, explain ownership and aliasing, and compare semantic results before measuring storage behavior.
key_terms: Creating output buffers once outside a loop and filling them in place, so repeated iterations do not allocate.
The in-place product `mul!(C, A, B)` that writes into an existing `C`, which must not alias `A` or `B`.
Slices taken with `view` or `@views` that read and write the parent array without copying it.
A conservative overlap check that can flag possible sharing, so a true result means investigate rather than proven overlap.
Keeping a scratch buffer across calls of one computation, which is safe only when no other task uses it concurrently.
approach: `affine!` validates before it writes: the matrix width must equal the input length, the matrix height must equal the destination and bias lengths, and `Base.mightalias` must find no shared storage between the destination and any input. Only then does `mul!` overwrite the destination and `.+=` add the bias, so a rejected call leaves the output untouched.

exercises.title: Trace a matrix step
exercises.task: Compute the two entries before running the first case.
exercises.hint: Multiply rows by the input, then add bias.
exercises.why: With `[2 1; 0 3]` and input `[3, 4]`, the products are 6 + 4 = 10 and 0 + 12 = 12, and adding `[1, -1]` gives `[11, 11]`.
exercises.wrong: Multiplying column by column with the input transposed gives different entries and hides the row and column meaning.
exercises.verify: Example A asserts `destination == [11, 11]` and that `affine!` returns the same object with `===`.

exercises.title: Repeat with new inputs
exercises.answer: Multiplication overwrites both entries before adding the bias.
exercises.why: For input `[1, 2]` the products are 4 and 6, and adding the bias gives `[5, 5]`, fully replacing the earlier `[11, 11]`.
exercises.wrong: Accumulating into the destination with `+=` instead of `mul!` would add the new products to the old output.
exercises.verify: Example A asserts `destination == [5, 5]` after the second call.

exercises.title: Debug a width mismatch
exercises.task: Pass a 2-by-3 matrix and a length 2 input.
exercises.answer: The declared matrix width must equal input length; validation preserves the previous output here.
exercises.why: A 2 by 3 matrix needs an input of length 3, so the first check throws `DimensionMismatch` before `mul!` runs.
exercises.wrong: Validating after the multiplication could leave the destination half written when the error is raised.
exercises.verify: The reference fills the output with 7, makes the bad call and asserts `output == [7, 7]` afterward.

exercises.title: Find view overlap
exercises.task: Explain why two different view objects can be unsafe.
exercises.expected: They may address the same parent elements.
exercises.hint: Object identity is weaker than storage independence.
exercises.answer: The rejection uses mightalias, which conservatively checks possible shared storage.
exercises.why: `view(storage, 1:2)` and `view(storage, 2:3)` are different objects that both include `storage[2]`, so writing one changes what the other reads.
exercises.wrong: Checking `destination !== input` passes for two distinct views and misses the shared element.
exercises.verify: Example B asserts `@test_throws ArgumentError` for these views and that `storage == snapshot` after the rejection.

exercises.title: Design scratch ownership
exercises.task: Describe a safe interface for repeated calls that must permit overlapping inputs.
exercises.expected: Use a documented private scratch copy before mutation.
exercises.answer: A scratch buffer can preserve the original input, but its owner and lifetime must be explicit.
exercises.why: Copying the possibly overlapping input into an owned scratch buffer before writing removes the shared read and write.
exercises.wrong: Sharing one global scratch buffer among concurrent callers trades an aliasing bug for a race.
exercises.verify: Document who owns the scratch buffer, then test an overlapping call against the result computed on separate copies.

exercises.title: Evaluate a speed claim
exercises.task: Explain why fewer measured bytes may not mean faster code.
exercises.expected: Access patterns, dispatch and workload sizes also matter.
exercises.answer: Allocation is one measurement. End-to-end timing and correctness remain necessary.
exercises.why: Views can have strided access, and a call with fewer allocated bytes can still run slower on a different access pattern or size.
exercises.wrong: Treating `@allocated` returning a small number as a speedup claim skips the timing and correctness checks.
exercises.verify: Compare correct results first, then time warmed calls at several sizes and record bytes and seconds together.
